title: Reasons beside every step, and the extreme one that talks
summary: Prove the geometry instead of tasting it: angles chased with a named reason beside every move, polygon totals cut out of triangles, and the Pythagorean theorem spent straight away on real distance. Then extremal round two, working beside the number that only falls, with one problem that needs both tools at once.
materials: jumbo sidewalk chalk and the chalk grid on the driveway
paper, a ruler and a protractor
scissors and two sheets of squared paper for the cut-and-rearrange proof
a stack of scrap paper for the month's monster, because the small factorials get worked out by hand

problems.prompt: A full-size football pitch is about 100 metres long and 70 metres wide. Chalk the whole of it into squares half a metre across. About how many squares is that?
explanation: Half-metre squares means two to the metre, so 100 metres of length is 200 squares.
The 70 metres of width is 140 squares.
200 rows of 140 squares is 28,000, which rounds to about 30,000.
problems.useAgain: when a rectangle has to be counted in tiles and you know only its two sides and the size of one tile.
hints: How many half-metre squares fit along the 100-metre side?
Do the same across the 70-metre side, then multiply your two counts.
problems.socraticHint: If you halved the width of every square, would the number of squares double, or do something bigger?

variant.prompt: The same pitch chalked into squares one metre across instead. About how many squares is that?

problems.prompt: Suppose a program looks at every pair of 2,000 cows. About how many pairs is that?
explanation: Each cow can be paired with the 1,999 others, so counting outwards from everybody gives about 2,000 lots of 2,000, which is 4 million.
Every pair turned up twice that way, once from each end.
Halve it, and about 2 million pairs is the honest answer.
problems.useAgain: when a count runs outwards from every member of a group and each pair gets counted from both ends.
hints: Start with one cow. How many partners does she have?
Do it for all of them first, then ask how many times each pair was counted.
problems.socraticHint: If you list the pair Bessie and Elsie, whose list does that same pair also sit on?

variant.prompt: Suppose the program looks at every pair of 20,000 cows. About how many pairs is that?

problems.prompt: The grader allows a C++ program 2 seconds on one test. Take this season's own measured figure, about a hundred million simple steps a second. About how many steps fit inside that limit?
explanation: A hundred million steps in one second is the figure you timed yourself in week 3.
Two seconds is two lots of that.
Two hundred million steps, which is far more room than a Bronze farm ever asks for.
problems.useAgain: when a speed you measured yourself has to be stretched across a limit somebody else set.
hints: Work out one second first, then the second one.
Use your own timed number rather than a number you were handed.
problems.socraticHint: Which number here did you measure and which did somebody tell you? Should you trust them the same amount?

variant.prompt: The same grader allows a Python program 4 seconds. Take about ten million simple steps a second. About how many steps fit inside that limit?

problem.prompt: On the driveway you chalk a right triangle with legs 6 feet and 8 feet, then chalk a square standing outward on each of its three sides. What is the total area of the three squares, in square feet?
explanation: The square on the 6 side has area 36, and the square on the 8 side has area 64.
The third side is the long one. 36 plus 64 is 100, so that side is 10 and its square has area 100.
36 plus 64 plus 100 is 200.
A shortcut was sitting in the picture. The big square is always the two small ones put together, so the total is twice the big one.
problem.useAgain: when squares, areas or straight-line distances hang off the sides of a right triangle.
hints: Chalk it for real. The square on a side of length 6 is 6 feet by 6 feet.
Work out the third side before you try to draw its square.
problem.socraticHint: Look at your three areas. Is one of them doing on its own what the other two are doing together?

variant.prompt: You chalk a right triangle with legs 5 feet and 12 feet and a square standing outward on each side. What is the total area of the three squares, in square feet?

steps.title: The geometry block, with a reason beside every step

problems.prompt:
Two parallel rails are crossed by one straight post. Below the top rail and to the right of the post, the angle is 70 degrees. Idris found the angle above the bottom rail and to the right of the post like this:
Line 1: The 70 degree angle sits below the top rail and to the right of the post. The angle I want sits above the bottom rail and to the right of the post.
Line 2: Those two angles are in alternate positions, so they are alternate angles.
Line 3: Alternate angles on parallel lines are equal, so the angle above the bottom rail and to the right of the post is 70 degrees.
Line 4: Check: that angle and the one beside it along the bottom rail add to 180, so the angle above the bottom rail and to the left of the post is 110 degrees.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 2 is wrong: this pair sits on the same side of the post, which makes them co-interior angles, not alternate ones.
Alternate angles sit on opposite sides of the post, one below one rail and one above the other.
Co-interior angles on parallel lines add to 180, they do not stay equal.
So the angle above the bottom rail and to the right of the post is 110 degrees, not 70.
Line 1 correctly names both positions.
Line 4 correctly follows from Line 3's wrong number, but on its own it does not reveal that Line 3 was wrong.
problems.useAgain: when two angles are named by their position across parallel lines, and you have to get the pairing right before you get the rule right.
hints: Decide whether the two angles sit on the same side of the crossing line or on opposite sides before naming the pair.
Same side and opposite side are not the same pairing, and they do not follow the same rule.
problems.socraticHint: Which of alternate and co-interior angles sit on the same side of the crossing post, and which sit on opposite sides?

variant.prompt:
Two straight roads cross. One angle at the crossing is 55 degrees. Marisol found the angle right beside it like this:
Line 1: The angle beside the 55 degree angle sits directly across the crossing from it.
Line 2: Angles directly across a crossing from each other are called opposite angles, and opposite angles are equal.
Line 3: So the angle beside the 55 degree angle is also 55 degrees.
Line 4: Check: an angle and its true opposite always look the same size when you compare them across the crossing, and that matches.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Two straight lines cross at a point, making four angles in order around the crossing: angle 1, angle 2, angle 3, angle 4. Angle 1 and angle 3 sit directly opposite each other, and so do angle 2 and angle 4. Using only the fact that angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees, write a two-column proof that angle 1 equals angle 3. State each step and the reason beside it.

mustMention: angle 1 and angle 2 form a linear pair, so they add to 180
angle 2 and angle 3 also form a linear pair, so they add to 180
both sums equal 180, so angle 1 plus angle 2 equals angle 2 plus angle 3
subtracting angle 2 from both sides leaves angle 1 equals angle 3

explanation: A two-column proof lines up statements with the reason for each one beside it, the reasons-beside-every-step idea taken all the way.
Angle 1 and angle 2 sit on a straight line. Their reason is angles on a straight line, so angle 1 plus angle 2 equals 180.
Angle 2 and angle 3 also sit on a straight line, giving angle 2 plus angle 3 equals 180 for the same reason.
Both sums equal 180, so angle 1 plus angle 2 equals angle 2 plus angle 3.
Subtract angle 2 from both sides and angle 1 equals angle 3.
problems.useAgain: when you need to justify every step of a claim, not just state the final angle.
hints: Chalk two straight lines crossing and mark the four angles in order. Two of your four angles already sit on a straight line together.
Write two separate linear-pair equations first, one for each straight line, before you try to connect them.
problems.socraticHint: If two different sums both equal 180, what does that tell you about those two sums compared to each other?

problems.prompt: Two fence rails run parallel across the yard and one straight post crosses both. Where the post meets the top rail, the angle above the rail and to the right of the post is 62 degrees. At the bottom rail, how many degrees is the angle in the matching corner, above the rail and to the right of the post?
explanation: The two corners sit in the same position at their own rail: both above, both to the right.
The rails are parallel, so the post leans across both of them at exactly the same tilt.
Matching corners on parallel lines are equal, so the answer is 62. That sentence is the reason, and it goes beside the step.
problems.useAgain: when a line crosses two parallel lines and one angle at one of the crossings is known.
hints: Mark both crossings and say out loud where each angle sits: above or below, left or right.
Ask what stays the same about the post's tilt at each rail, and what makes that true.
problems.socraticHint: If the two rails were not parallel, could you still say anything at all about the second angle?

variant.prompt: The angle above the top rail and to the right of the post is 74 degrees. How many degrees is the angle in the matching corner at the bottom rail?

problems.prompt: Two parallel rails, one post crossing both. At the top rail the angle on the right of the post and below the rail is 118 degrees. Its alternate angle at the bottom rail, on the left of the post and above the rail, is 118 too. How many degrees is the angle right beside that one along the bottom rail?
explanation: Step one, and its reason: alternate angles on parallel lines are equal, so the bottom one is 118.
The angle asked for sits beside that 118, so the two lie on one straight line.
Step two, and its reason: angles on a straight line. 180 take away 118 is 62.
A chase with a reason missing has to be done again by somebody else.
problems.useAgain: when an angle takes more than one step to reach and each step leans on a different rule.
hints: Do it in two moves and do not try to see the answer in one.
Write the reason for the first move down before you start the second.
problems.socraticHint: Which of your two moves needed the rails to be parallel, and which would have worked on any straight line at all?

variant.prompt: The alternate angle at the bottom rail is 143 degrees. How many degrees is the angle right beside it along the bottom rail?

problems.prompt: Two seasons ago you tore the three corners off a paper triangle and they lay flat in a straight line. Using that, how many degrees do the six inside angles of a hexagon add to?
explanation: From one corner, draw a line to each corner that is not a neighbour. That cuts the hexagon into 4 triangles.
Every triangle holds 180 degrees, which is what the torn corners showed when they lay flat.
4 lots of 180 is 720.
The triangles use up the hexagon's own corners exactly, nothing extra and nothing missing.
problems.useAgain: when a many-sided shape needs its angle total and you can cut it into triangles from one corner.
hints: Do not count angles. Count triangles first.
Draw a hexagon and cut it from a single corner, then see how many triangles you actually got.
problems.socraticHint: How many triangles came out of the hexagon, and how does that number sit next to its six sides?

variant.prompt: How many degrees do the inside angles of a ten-sided shape add to?

problems.prompt: A regular octagon has eight equal sides and eight equal inside angles. How many degrees is one of those angles?
explanation: Cut it from one corner and you get 6 triangles, so the eight angles add to 1080.
Regular means all eight are the same size, so the total can be shared out equally.
1080 shared among 8 is 135.
Regular is the word that earns the sharing step. Without it, one angle could be anything.
problems.useAgain: when a shape is regular and its angle total has to be turned into one single angle.
hints: Get the total for all eight angles before you go anywhere near one of them.
Ask which word in the question lets you divide, and underline it.
problems.socraticHint: What would break in your working if the eight sides were not all the same length?

variant.prompt: A regular ten-sided shape has ten equal sides and ten equal inside angles. How many degrees is one of those angles?

problems.prompt: A ladder 26 feet long leans against a wall with its foot 10 feet out from the base of the wall. How many feet up the wall does the top of the ladder reach?
explanation: The wall, the ground and the ladder make a right triangle, and the ladder is the long side.
The two small squares fill the big one, so the missing square is 26 squared take away 10 squared.
676 take away 100 is 576, and 24 times 24 is 576, so the ladder reaches 24 feet up.
problems.useAgain: when a right triangle is missing a short side and the long one is the side you already know.
hints: Which of the three sides is the long one here? It is not the side the question asks about.
Take away rather than add, because this time you are hunting one of the small squares.
problems.socraticHint: You know the big square and one small square. What does that leave for the other small one?

variant.prompt: A ladder 15 feet long leans against a wall with its foot 9 feet out. How many feet up the wall does the top reach?

problems.prompt: On the jumbo chalk grid on the driveway, one flag stands at the point (2, 3) and another at (7, 15). How many steps apart are they in a straight line?
explanation: Across from 2 to 7 is 5 steps. Up from 3 to 15 is 12 steps.
Those two walks meet at a square corner, so the straight line is the long side of a triangle with legs 5 and 12.
25 plus 144 is 169, and 13 times 13 is 169, so the answer is 13.
Every straight-line distance on a map is a triangle you can build.
problems.useAgain: when two points on a grid or a map need the straight distance between them rather than the walk.
hints: Do not measure it. Work out the across first, then the up.
Draw the right triangle those two walks make and label its two legs.
problems.socraticHint: Why is the straight line always shorter than walking across and then up, and could the two ever be equal?

variant.prompt: One flag stands at (1, 2) and another at (9, 17). How many steps apart are they in a straight line?

steps.title: One angle copied across parallel lines, and more from the shop's table

problems.prompt: Line m is parallel to line n. A transversal crosses both, making a 70 degree angle with line m at the upper right. What is the corresponding angle at line n, also at the upper right, in degrees?
explanation: A transversal crossing two parallel lines copies each angle to the matching corner at the other line.
The upper-right angle at line n sits in the exact same corner position as the one at line m.
Corresponding angles like these are always equal, so it is also 70 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when two parallel lines are cut by the same transversal, and an angle needs copying to its matching corner.
hints: Which corner position at line n matches the corner position given at line m?
Corresponding angles at the same corner position are always equal on parallel lines.
problems.socraticHint: If the two lines are truly parallel, why would the transversal cross them at anything but the same angle each time?

variant.prompt: Line m is parallel to line n. A transversal makes a 118 degree angle with line m at the upper right. What is the corresponding angle at line n, in degrees?

problems.prompt: Lines m and n are parallel. A transversal makes a 65 degree angle with line m. That transversal and line n also form a triangle, whose third angle (not touching the transversal or line n) measures 40 degrees. What is the triangle's angle at line n, in degrees?
explanation: The transversal's angle at line n, alternate to the 65 degree angle, is also 65 degrees.
That is because alternate angles on parallel lines are always equal.
The triangle's three angles still add to 180: 65 plus 40 is 105.
180 minus 105 is 75 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when a parallel-line angle fact hands you one triangle angle for free, and the triangle sum finishes the job.
hints: Which angle fact from the parallel lines gives you the triangle's angle at line n before you even use the triangle sum?
Add the two known triangle angles, then subtract from 180.
problems.socraticHint: Once the parallel-line fact hands you one of the triangle's three angles, what tool finds the last one?

variant.prompt: Lines m and n are parallel. A transversal makes a 50 degree angle with line m. That transversal and line n form a triangle whose third angle measures 60 degrees. What is the triangle's angle at line n, in degrees?

problems.prompt: Using the shop records (15 under-20 bought A, 25 under-20 bought B, 30 aged 20+ bought A, 30 aged 20+ bought B), of everyone who bought product A, what fraction were 20 or older?
explanation: The condition here is buying product A, so only A buyers count in the whole.
Total A buyers is 15 plus 30, which is 45.
Those 20 or older among them is 30, so the fraction is 30/45, which simplifies to 2/3.
problems.useAgain: when the condition is which product was bought, so only buyers of that one product form the whole.
hints: Find the total number of product A buyers first, ignoring age.
Put the 20-or-older count among them over that total.
problems.socraticHint: Does the number of product B buyers matter at all for this question about product A buyers?

variant.prompt: Using shop records where 10 under-20 and 40 aged 20+ bought product A, of everyone who bought product A, what fraction were 20 or older?

problems.prompt: Using the same shop records, of everyone 20 or older, what fraction bought product B?
explanation: The condition is being 20 or older, so only that age group forms the whole.
Total 20-or-older customers is 30 plus 30, which is 60.
Those who bought B among them is 30, so the fraction is 30/60, which is 1/2.
problems.useAgain: when the condition is an age group instead of a product, changing which total you divide by.
hints: Find the total number of 20-or-older customers first.
Put the product B count among them over that total.
problems.socraticHint: Does the under-20 group matter at all once the condition restricts you to the 20-or-older group?

variant.prompt: Using shop records where 20+ bought A is 40 and 20+ bought B is 20, of everyone 20 or older, what fraction bought product B?

figure.alt: White to move. A white queen on d1 faces a black rook on a6, with the black king on a8 on the same file.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move pins the black rook to its king?
explanation: Black's king on a8 and rook on a6 share the same open file.
Qa4 lines the queen up on that file, right behind the rook.
The rook cannot step off that file without leaving its king in check.
problems.useAgain: when an enemy piece and its king share an open file your queen can reach.
hints: Which file already holds both the black king and the black rook?
Move your queen onto that same file, behind the rook.
problems.socraticHint: If the rook slid sideways right now, what would happen to the king?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move pins the black rook to its king?

figure.alt: White to move. A white queen on e4 faces a black rook on h6, with the black king on h8 on the same file.
White to move. A white bishop on c1 faces two undefended black rooks on d8 and h4.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move attacks two black rooks at once?
explanation: A bishop landing on g5 attacks both d8 and h4 along its two diagonals.
Black's two rooks sit on exactly those squares with no defender.
Black can only save one rook.
problems.useAgain: when one bishop move covers two different diagonals, each hitting an undefended piece.
hints: Find a bishop square that looks two different ways at once.
Check both diagonals from that square for black pieces.
problems.socraticHint: If black saves one rook, what happens to the other?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move attacks two black rooks at once?

figure.alt: White to move. A white bishop on f1 faces two undefended black rooks on a4 and d7.
White to move. Black's lone king sits on h8, a white rook on b7 seals off the seventh rank, and a white rook on a1 stands ready.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?
explanation: Your rook on b7 already covers every square on the seventh rank.
Ra8 checks the king along the back rank, and the seventh rank is sealed off too.
The king has no square anywhere near it, so it is mate.
problems.useAgain: when one rook seals off a whole rank while the other delivers check on the next one.
hints: What does your rook on the seventh rank already control?
Find the other rook move that checks the king on the back rank.
problems.socraticHint: Could the black king step down a rank to escape the check?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?

figure.alt: White to move. Black's lone king sits on a8, a white rook on g7 seals off the seventh rank, and a white rook on h1 stands ready.
White to move. A white rook on a1 faces a black queen alone on a6.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move wins the undefended black queen?
explanation: Black's queen sits alone on a6 with no defender.
The white rook already shares that file.
Rxa6 wins the queen for a rook, the biggest trade on the board.
problems.useAgain: when the biggest piece on the board has nobody watching its back.
hints: Which black piece is worth the most, and does anything defend it?
Which white piece already shares a file with it?
problems.socraticHint: Which black piece would black least want to lose for nothing?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move wins the undefended black queen?

steps.title: The extreme one, and the number that only falls

problems.prompt: Five cows stand in a field and every distance between two of them is different from every other distance. Each cow moos once, at whichever cow is nearest to her. True or false: it is possible that every cow gets mooed at.
explanation: Start at the extreme. Find the two cows standing closer together than any other pair in the field.
Each is the other's nearest, so they moo at each other and need nobody else.
That leaves three cows and three moos. To cover all three, those three must moo round in a ring.
Then the first distance is under the second, the second under the third, the third under the first. Shorter than itself.
So somebody gets nothing, and the extreme pair is what cracked it.
problems.useAgain: when a problem hands you many things and no picture, and one of them is the biggest, smallest, first or closest.
hints: Which two cows in the whole field can you be sure about without seeing where anybody stands?
Find the shortest distance in the field and ask who each of those two cows moos at.
problems.socraticHint: Two of the five are already settled. What are the other three forced to do with their three moos?

variant.prompt: Four cows stand in a field, all the distances different, each mooing at her nearest. True or false: it is possible that every cow gets mooed at.

problems.prompt: A bowl holds 20 sweets. A move takes two sweets out and drops one back in. Moves go on until a single sweet is left. How many moves is that?
explanation: Each move removes two and returns one, so the bowl loses exactly one sweet every single move.
Going from 20 down to 1 is 19 steps down.
Which sweets got picked never mattered. The count only falls, one at a time, toward a wall it cannot pass, so the ending was fixed before the first move.
problems.useAgain: when every move changes some count in the same direction and you need to know the thing ends.
hints: Do not follow the sweets. Follow how many are in the bowl.
Work out what one move does to that number, then ask how far the number has to travel.
problems.socraticHint: Is there anything a player could do to make this last longer, or finish sooner?

variant.prompt: A bowl holds 50 sweets and the same move is used. How many moves until a single sweet is left?

problems.prompt: The numbers 12 and 18 are written on a board. A move rubs out the larger one and writes in its place the larger take away the smaller. When the two numbers are equal the game stops. What number do they stop on?
explanation: Play it: 18 and 12 becomes 12 and 6, and 12 and 6 becomes 6 and 6. It stops on 6.
Why it must stop: watch the larger one. Every move replaces it with something smaller, and whole numbers above zero cannot fall forever.
Why 6: a number dividing both also divides their difference, so a move never destroys a shared divisor. 6 divided both at the start.
Neither tool works alone. The extreme one says what to watch, the falling says it ends.
problems.useAgain: when a rule keeps replacing the biggest thing with something smaller and you have to say where it lands.
hints: Play the moves out on paper first. Three lines is enough to see the ending.
Then ask which of the two numbers you should be watching, and what every move does to it.
problems.socraticHint: What is true of both numbers at the start that is still true at every stage, however many moves have gone by?

variant.prompt: The numbers 20 and 35 are written on a board and the same move is used. What number do they stop on?

problems.prompt: Nine cows stand in a 3 by 3 pen, all of different weights. In each row, mark the heaviest cow, then call the lightest of those three marked cows A. Start again: in each column, mark the lightest cow, then call the heaviest of those three B. Which of these is true?
options: B is always heavier than A.
A is always at least as heavy as B.
Which one is heavier depends on how the cows are arranged.
explanation: A is the heaviest cow in her own row. B is the lightest in her own column.
Look at the one cow standing where A's row meets B's column, and call her M.
A is heaviest in that row, so A is at least as heavy as M. B is lightest in her column, so B is no heavier.
So A is at least as heavy as B, whatever the arrangement.
The trap is the wording: A came off a list of heaviest cows, B off a list of lightest.
problems.useAgain: when two extremes are built out of the same grid and you have to compare them without checking every case.
hints: A stands somewhere in the pen and so does B. Which single cow stands where A's row meets B's column?
Compare that middle cow with A, then compare her with B, and put the two facts side by side.
problems.socraticHint: You now have two facts about one cow nobody asked about. What do they say when you read them together?

variant.prompt: Sixteen cows stand in a 4 by 4 pen, all of different weights, and A and B are built in exactly the same way. Which of these is true?
options: Which one is heavier depends on how the cows are arranged.
B is always heavier than A.
A is always at least as heavy as B.

problems.prompt: Five different positive whole numbers add up to 20. What is the biggest that any one of them can be?
explanation: To push one of them as high as it will go, push the other four as low as they will go.
They must be different positive whole numbers, so the smallest four are 1, 2, 3 and 4, adding to 10.
That leaves 20 take away 10, which is 10.
Check it is legal. The list 1, 2, 3, 4, 10 is five different numbers adding to 20.
problems.useAgain: when a question asks how big one thing can be and the rest of the pieces are free to move.
hints: If one number is to be huge, what has to be true of the others?
Write down the four smallest different positive whole numbers there are, and add them.
problems.socraticHint: Why can the other four not simply be 1, 1, 1 and 1?

variant.prompt: Four different positive whole numbers add up to 20. What is the biggest that any one of them can be?

problems.prompt: Five different positive whole numbers have a mean of 10 and a median of 9. What is the biggest that the largest of them can be?
explanation: A mean of 10 across five numbers means they add to 50. A median of 9 pins the middle one at 9.
To send the top number as high as it goes, drive every other number as low as it goes.
The two below the middle are different whole numbers under 9, so they are 1 and 2.
The one just above the middle must be over 9, so it is 10.
1 plus 2 plus 9 plus 10 is 22, and 50 take away 22 is 28.
problems.useAgain: when a mean and a middle are both fixed and the question asks how far one end can be pushed.
hints: Turn the mean into a total before anything else.
The median pins one number exactly. Ask what the smallest legal values on either side of it are.
problems.socraticHint: Which numbers in this list are you allowed to choose, and which one has already been chosen for you?

variant.prompt: Five different positive whole numbers have a mean of 10 and a median of 8. What is the biggest that the largest of them can be?

problems.prompt: A peak, untimed. A ladder 25 feet long leans against a wall with its foot 7 feet out from the wall. The foot slides out until it is 20 feet from the wall. How many feet does the top of the ladder come down?
explanation: The ladder never changes length, so both pictures are right triangles with a long side of 25, and 25 times 25 is 625.
Before the slide the foot is 7 out. 625 take away 49 leaves 576, so the top sits 24 up the wall.
After the slide the foot is 20 out. 625 take away 400 leaves 225, so the top sits 15 up.
From 24 up to 15 up is a fall of 9 feet.
The tempting answer is 13, the distance the foot travelled. Nothing makes the two agree.
problems.useAgain: when one side of a right triangle keeps its length while the other two change, and you are asked how far something moved.
hints: It is the same ladder in both pictures, so the long side of the triangle has not changed.
Work out how far up the wall the top sits before the slide, then again after it, and put the two heights side by side.
problems.socraticHint: The foot travelled a long way out. Is there any reason the top has to travel that same distance down?

variant.prompt: A peak, untimed. A ladder 25 feet long leans against a wall with its foot 7 feet out from the wall. The foot slides out until it is 15 feet from the wall. How many feet does the top of the ladder come down?

problems.prompt: A second peak, untimed. Ten stones sit in one pile. A move splits one pile into two smaller piles, and it scores the two new sizes multiplied together. Keep going until every pile is a single stone. What is the biggest total score you can end with?
explanation: Play it twice, splitting differently each time, and the two totals come out equal. That is the clue.
Count the pairs of stones still sharing a pile. At the start that is ten times nine halved, which is 45.
At the end every stone stands alone, so not one pair is still sharing.
Split the ten into a four and a six. That separates four times six pairs, and 24 is exactly what the move scores.
So every move scores the pairs it breaks up, and each pair gets broken up once and never again.
The total is 45 by every route. The biggest is 45, and so is the smallest.
problems.useAgain: when a game asks for the biggest total you can reach and you suspect every way of playing it ends in the same place.
hints: Play the whole game out with four stones, twice, choosing different splits, and compare the two totals.
Every move separates some pairs of stones that were sharing a pile. Count how many pairs one move separates.
problems.socraticHint: Pick two particular stones and follow them to the end. On how many of your moves do those two get separated?

variant.prompt: A second peak, untimed. Eight stones sit in one pile. A move splits one pile into two smaller piles, and it scores the two new sizes multiplied together. Keep going until every pile is a single stone. What is the biggest total score you can end with?

problems.prompt: Write up, so that somebody else could read it and be convinced, why the two closest cows in a field always moo at each other. Say what you are assuming about the distances, give the argument, and finish with the sentence this week keeps making about the extreme thing.

mustMention: the two cows whose distance is the shortest in the whole field
no other cow is nearer to either of them than they are to each other
so each one of the pair is the other's nearest
the extreme one has nowhere to hide

explanation: Most of the work is writing down what closest pair promises: their distance beats every other distance in the field.
So a third cow nearer to one of them would be a distance smaller than the smallest, which cannot exist.
That leaves each of the two with the other as her nearest, so both moos land inside the pair.
Every extremal argument has this shape: pick the extreme thing, then show it has no room left.
problems.useAgain: when you have to say why the biggest, smallest or nearest thing in a problem behaves the way it does.
hints: Begin by writing down what closest pair in the field promises you about every other pair.
Suppose one of the two had a nearer neighbour, and see what that does to your first sentence.
problems.socraticHint: What exactly would have to exist for the claim to fail, and could that thing live in the same field?

steps.title: The month 2 monster opens: the zeros on the end of 100 factorial
steps.body:
A monster is not a lesson. It goes on the home card, it stays there for the month, and it is yours to circle, poke and leave alone for days. Nobody is going to teach it to you.

Here it is. 100 factorial means 100 times 99 times 98, all the way down to 1. It is a colossal number and nobody wants you to work it out. Written out in full it ends in a run of zeros. How many zeros are on the end, and why exactly that many?

Start small, the way you always do. Work out 5 factorial by hand, then 6, then 10. Write them in the journal with their zeros counted, and watch when the count goes up and when it refuses to.

One thing worth asking early, and it is a question rather than a hint: what has to happen inside a multiplication for a zero to appear on the end at all? Two seasons ago you learned that every number is built out of primes in exactly one way. That fact is standing right next to this problem.

A warning about the obvious road. You could ask Python to work out 100 factorial and count the zeros on the screen, and it will do it happily, because Python's whole numbers have no walls. That is a fine thing to do once and it answers how many. It does not answer why exactly that many, which is the actual monster. If you go that way, go that way second.

This one stays open past this week. Nobody is asking you for it today.

steps.title: The cut-and-rearrange proof, written so you could defend it
steps.prompt: Cut two squares of squared paper the same size. On the first, lay four copies of one right triangle in the corners so that the space left empty in the middle is a single square standing on the long side. On the second, lay the same four triangles a different way so the empty space is two squares, one on each short side. Then write the proof out: what is the same about the two big squares, what is the same about the eight triangles, and what that forces about the space left over. A reason beside every step. Finish by saying what would break in the argument if the triangle did not have a square corner.

steps.title: Say the extremal argument out loud
steps.prompt: Two minutes, standing, no paper. Tell the cow field problem to somebody who has not seen it. Say what the extreme thing is, why you looked there first, and where the argument runs out of room. Then answer one question they ask you about it.
